list.listitem: Cleft lip (CL) and cleft palate (CP) are common congenital defects and their cause is multifactorial. Phenytoin and cigarette smoking are two of the most consistent risk factors. B
Squeezable bottles containing breast milk or breastfeeding are preferred feeding options. B
All infants with clefts require a thorough head and neck evaluation to the tip of the uvula. C
Children with clefts should be evaluated and treated by a special CL/CP "team." C
Pre-operative nasoalveolar molding may improve aesthetic outcomes. B

Surgical repair is the mainstay of therapy. C Early closure at 6 instead of 12 months of age for children with nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate may confer benefit for later speech (fewer with velopharyngeal insufficiency). B
Speech therapy appears helpful. B

background.definition: Failure of closure of craniofacial tissues during fetal development can result in a wide spectrum of possible presentations including CL with or without CP, or CP alone. There are several classification systems for CL/P; one is shown in Table 1.

list.listitem: Overall: 1.4 per 1000 live births.
Asian: 2.1 per 1000.
Native American: 3.6 per 1000.
African American: 0.3 per 1000.
Caucasian: 1 per 1000.
Gender: 2:1 male to female ratio for clefts involving the lip and approximately a 1:2 male to female ratio for clefts of the palate only.
Global prevalence of CP, based on a meta-analysis of 59 studies with over 21 million individuals, was 0.33 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28-0.38) per 1000 live births.

Global prevalence of CL, based on a meta-analysis of 57 studies with over 17 million individuals, was 0.3 (95%CI 0.26-0.34) per 1000 live births; for both CL/CP, overall prevalence was 0.45 (95%CI 0.38-0.52) per 1000 live births.
Authors of a meta-analysis found that unaffected parents have a constellation of subtle yet consistent facial abnormalities.

Children with cleft lips/palates have an increased risk of congenital heart disease with an overall pooled estimate of 16% (95% CI 13-19%). The odds of developing CHD for those with cleft palate was 4.1 (95% CI 3.9-4.3) compared to cleft lip alone and 1.7 (95% CI 1.5-1.7) compared to those with both cleft lip and palate.
In a retrospective chart review of 459 patients with CP, there was a high incidence of sleep-disordered breathing and polysomnography-diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea (37.5% and 8.5%, respectively).
Most children with CP develop otitis media with effusion (OME). In a study of 95 Thai children with CP, cumulative incidence of OME was 53.7% by 12 months and 81.1% by 24 months of age.

In a study of 52 children with CP who underwent Furlow-type palatoplasty, resolution of persistent OME followed an age-related pattern and occurred in 4.4% before age 1 year, 10.9% by age 1 year, 21.7% by age 2 years, 37% by age 3 years, 50% by age 4 years, and 60.9% by age 5 years.

Children with non-syndromic orofacial clefts have a high incidence of dental anomalies including microdontia (OR 14.8, 95% CI, 4.0 to 54.6), agenesis (OR 14.2, 95% CI, 9.4 to 21.3), peg-shaped anterior teeth (OR 12.2, 95% CI, 3.6 to 41.2), supernumerary teeth (OR 5.7, 95% CI, 3.3 to 9.7), developmental enamel defects (OR 5.6, 95% CI, 3.5 to 9.0), tooth malposition and/or transposition (OR 5.6, 95% CI, 2.8 to 11.5), tooth rotation (OR 3.2, 95% CI, 1.3 to 8.2), and tooth impaction (OR 3.6, 95% CI, 1.1 to 12.2).They also have a higher risk of dental caries (64% vs. 52% for those without cleft lip/palate).
Individuals with CL/CP also have a significantly increased number of cervical vertebrae anomalies compared to those without CL/CP (OR 2.63, 95% CI 2.15-3.22), based on a meta-analysis of 10 studies.

Children born with cleft lip and/or palate appear to have similar psychological outcomes compared to normative controls, although some emotional symptoms such as anxiety and depression may be higher in these children based on a meta-analysis of 9 studies.
Up to 30% of cases with CL with or without CP and 50% of cases of CP are associated with a syndrome.

Non-syndromic complex genetic mutations have been described with multiple loci implicated. Some cases of CL/CP have been associated with a mutation of the TGFA Taq1 C2 allele; the best evidence has been reported for mutations in MSX1 (msh homeobox 1), FGFR1 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 1), FGF8, and BMP4 (bone morphogenetic protein 4). Some gene polymorphisms are associated with a lower risk of non-syndromic CL as well.
A more recent study identified six additional susceptibility regions, and others continue to be identified.
Associated risk factors are shown in the table below.
Failure of closure of the facial clefts during the fourth through seventh weeks of embryologic development results in either CL, CP, or both. Clefts may be either unilateral, bilateral, or midline.
Most clefts are nonsyndromal and are felt to be multifactorial or the result of a mutation at a single gene locus.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Affected mother, father, or first-degree relative (CL)
Affected mother, father, or first-degree relative (CP)
Valproic acid use in first trimester pregnancy
Topiramate use in first trimester pregnancy
Amoxicillin use in third trimester (cleft lip with or without cleft palate)

list.listitem: Folic acid supplementation during pregnancy may have a protective benefit for oral clefts, but authors of a 2015 Cochrane review did not concur. B
Although the cause of many cases of CL and CP are unknown, cigarette smoking has consistently been implicated; smoking cessation prior to and during pregnancy should be encouraged. B

Avoid use of medications associated with CP if possible, especially use in the first trimester of pregnancy, or provide information about such risk; drugs include anti-epileptic agents and NSAIDs. In a recent population-based study, women exposed to ondansetron in the first trimester had an increased adjusted relative difference of oral clefts of 2.7 per 10,000 births (95% CI 0.2-5.2); NNTH = 3700.
Screening specifically for CL and CP is controversial and is not specifically addressed by major organizations outside of routine ultrasound screening recommendations.
Children with CL/P should receive dental care before 1 year of age as oral health can influence craniofacial treatment.
For children with CP and OME, ventilation tube insertion may be of benefit compared to watchful waiting for hearing recovery based on cohort studies.

Prenatal 2D ultrasound is moderately sensitive for CL but usually does not detect CP. Among high-risk fetuses, 3D ultrasound has high sensitivity and specificity for CP. B Prenatal MRI increases the likelihood of diagnosing palatal clefts if only CL is seen on ultrasound. B
Although CL may exist alone, it may be associated with genetic malformations, particularly if accompanied by CP. Amniocentesis should be offered in prenatal diagnoses of CP. B
All children with clefts need a thorough head and neck evaluation to the tip of the uvula. C
CL and CP are usually obvious at birth, but more subtle abnormalities, such as a submucosal cleft, may not be evident until the child presents with nasal speech.
Unilateral CL is associated with CP 68% of the time; bilateral CL has an 86% association with CP.
Nasal regurgitation during suckling may indicate CP and requires careful examination.
All infants with clefts should have a thorough head and neck evaluation to the tip of the uvula. The presence of a bifid uvula indicates a submucous CP.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies found that routine two-dimensional (2D) ultrasound (US) detected 362 of 1819 clefts for an overall sensitivity of 20% (range 13%-63%). There were 8 more false positives in a population of 5407, which could be psychologically damaging or lead to a decision to terminate the pregnancy.

In another meta-analysis, similar findings were reported for 2D ultrasound (9%-100% for CL with or without CP and 0%-22% for CP only); three-dimensional (3D) US in high-risk women improved detection rates for CL (100%) and CL with palate (86%-90%) but not for CP only (0%-89%). In 1 small study, 3D US by 4 readers had a sensitivity of cleft detection of 33% to 63% and a specificity of 84% to 95%; interrater reliability was 0.62 (95% CI, 0.47-0.76).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies involving 663 high-risk fetuses found that prenatal fetal 3D or 2D + 3D ultrasound accurately predicted CP with a pooled sensitivity of 87% (95% CI 71%-95%), specificity of 98% (95%CI 90%-100%), and area under the SROC curve of 0.98 (95% CI 0.97-0.99).
Prenatal MRI should be considered in cases where a prenatal diagnosis of CL has been made, as it may increase the likelihood of detecting palatal clefts if only CL is seen on ultrasound. B

In an RCT of 105 infants with cleft lip and palate undergoing CT scan prior to surgery, administration of combination intranasal dexmedetomidine 2 µg/kg with midazolam 0.05 mg/kg compared to dexmedetomidine alone resulted in higher sedation success and successful scans (95.9% vs. 80.4%), respectively, but had longer duration of sedation (80 min vs. 68.5 min) and longer recovery time (43 min vs. 31.5 min).

Most cases of CL with or without CP are isolated defects. The risk of associated genetic abnormalities depends on the type of cleft, with Type 2, 3, 4, and 5 clefts more likely to be associated with syndromic and other anomalies.
Risk of syndromic associations is 5% to 14%.
Van der Woude syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by CL and CP and blind sinus pits. A list of other syndromic disorders can be found in the article by Dixon and colleagues.
Pierre Robin sequence is a disorder in which CP can result from micrognathia (small jaw) which also creates backward placement of the tongue and can lead to airway obstruction.

As palatal clefts are difficult to detect prenatally and their presence indicates an increased risk of genetic abnormality, parents should be offered amniocentesis if a CL with or "without" CP is detected. Based on data from the Dutch Oral Cleft registry, in the absence of associated anomalies, prenatal karyotyping is not recommended in cleft lip as chromosomal defects were found in less than 2% of patients. With isolated cleft lip and palate or cleft palate (rates less than 4% in this study) or for patients with associated anomalies, prenatal invasive testing, preferably by array based methods is recommended.
Tympanometry may not be a reliable tool for evaluating otitis media with effusion (OME) in children younger than 9 months with CP, as it has low specificity in that age group.
Although routine ultrasound may detect abnormalities during second and third trimesters, CL and CP are usually detected at birth.
MRI can aid in further staging and characterizing the lesion, particularly palatal lesions.
A classification scheme for CL and CP is shown in .

Parent education for acceptance of pre-surgical nasoalveolar molding as a pre-surgical tool for cleft lip and palate-affected infants was enhanced using a virtual reality format in a small RCT including 20 parents/caregivers. In this study, all 12 participants in the virtual reality group were able to understand the doctor's explanation regarding molding compared to 33% in the conventional education module group.
Squeezable bottles are easier to use than rigid bottles, and breastfeeding or syringe feeding of breast milk results in greater weight gain (0.5 kg at 6 weeks) than spoon feeding. B
Children with clefts should be referred soon after birth for evaluation and treatment by a CL/CP team. C

Surgical correction is the mainstay of treatment. A Early closure at 6 months instead of 12 months of age for children with nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate may confer benefit for later speech (fewer with velopharyngeal insufficiency). B
Data are conflicting on benefits of presurgical orthopedic devices, although pre-operative nasoalveolar molding may improve aesthetic outcomes. B
Surgical repair is the mainstay of therapy. The need for alveolar bone grafting is determined by the degree of alveolar ridge notching.

Surgical repair is usually divided into 2 procedures, lip/hard palate and soft palatal closures. CL repair usually occurs between 2 and 6 months of age and primary palate repair at between 6 and 18 months.

The American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association (ACPA) provided guidance on safety and timing of surgical repairs during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most procedures could be safely delayed and non-surgical options pursued until bans on non-essential surgeries are lifted.

Surgical correction of CP is aimed at separating the oral and nasal cavities and usually includes levator muscle sling reconstitution. The surgical procedures include von Langenbeck (using bipedicle mucoperiosteal flaps), Schweckendiek (staged repair of soft and then hard palate), 2-flap, 3-flap (V-to-Y), and double-reverse z-plasty (Furlow; z-plasties of the soft palate mucosa and musculature) palatoplasties.

In 1 RCT, the Furlow z-palatoplasty resulted in significantly better velopharyngeal function for speech than the von Langenbeck procedure, but with a higher incidence of fistulas. In a systematic review of 12 studies, there was an increased incidence of secondary operations using a straight-line intravelar veloplasty repair of unilateral cleft lip-cleft palate compared with Furlow Z-plasty.

In a study of 291 patients with unilateral or bilateral complete CL/CP, surgery performed using the Veau-Wardill-Kilner palatoplasty with intravelar veloplasty and a conventional uvuloplasty (group A) resulted in more total complications than those performed using the Alveolar Extension Palatoplasty (Carsten's Variant, group B), with complete muscle dissection and retro positioning, plus posterior pillars elongation with hemi-uvula rotation and reconstruction (54.85% and 21.90%, respectively). Of note, although the same senior surgeon was involved in all cases, group A surgeries were conducted between 2002-2007 and group B between 2008-2013.

Surgery can be performed in 1 or 2 stages; in a 4-year follow-up study, 2-stage protocol was better with regard to maxillary growth, but there were no differences in the incidence of either velopharyngeal incompetence or articulation errors.
Outpatient CL repair appears safe, based on a meta-analysis of 6 studies, and does not increase readmission rates.

Submucosal cleft treatment depends on the severity of speech disturbance. Usually speech therapy is adequate, but pharyngoplasty is necessary if the palate cannot prevent air from escaping though the nose during speech (velopharyngeal incompetence) or if there are feeding or otologic problems.

Cochrane authors found only a single trial of low quality that demonstrated no significant difference comparing minimal incision palatopharyngoplasty with the same procedure performed simultaneously with an individually-tailored pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty for correcting velopharyngeal insufficiency associated with submucous cleft palate.

Authors of a meta-analysis of alveolar bone grafting for CL-CP concluded that grafting should occur before canine eruption with targeted preoperative orthopedic interventions, use of iliac crest corticocancellous autologous graft should continue, and adjunctive pain control methods should be used.

Authors of an attempted meta-analysis of early (age 5-6 years) vs. conventional (9-11 years) secondary alveolar bone grafting for CL/CP, were unable to find sufficient data to compare clinical outcomes.

The addition of advanced platelet rich fibrin to iliac bone graft for secondary alveolar bone grafting for patients with alveolar cleft may improve outcomes with respect to less bone resorption, based on preliminary data, and reduced scaring in those with CL. However, there was no benefit from use of platelet rich plasma/concentrate in percentage of alveolar cleft filled by a bone graft or bone formation based on 2 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs.

A 2009 guideline from the American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association recommends closure of CL before 12 months; surgery may be performed as soon as it is deemed safe for the infant. Closure of CP should occur before 18 months of age and ideally earlier.

In an RCT of 558 infants with nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate, those randomized to standardized primary surgical cleft closure at 6 months of age compared to 12 months of age were less likely to have velopharyngeal insufficiency, measured by speech recordings, at age 5 years (8.9% vs. 15.0%, respectively). Postoperative complications were infrequent and similar between groups, and the 4 serious adverse events (3 children in the 6-month group) had resolved at follow-up.

In the Scandcleft Trial 1, an RCT of 148 children with unilateral CL/CP in which all children received lip and velum closure at 4 months, there was no difference in speech outcomes between those randomized to hard palate closure at 12 months or 36 months. In the Scandcleft project trial 2 including 112 children with unilateral CL/CP, there were also no differences in speech outcomes for those randomized to either lip repair and soft palate closure at 4 months and hard palate closure at 12 months or lip repair at 3 to 4 months (Arm A), or a closure of both the soft and hard palate at 12 months.

Hard palate repair before 18 months is associated with less midface hypoplasia in adulthood. Sequence of the 2-stage palatal repair did not confer differences in speech outcomes in Scandcleft project trial 3.
Preoperative nasal swabs to guide antibiotic selection are not recommended by 2021 guidelines.
Allowing early/immediate postoperative breastfeeding or bottle-feeding does not increase dehiscence following CL repair (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.19-1.95).
A palatal block for postpalatoplasty analgesia was consistently better than no block or normal saline. In one RCT, bilateral suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block reduced post-operative morphine use.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 39 studies including 583 patients undergoing cleft lip repair and 1445 patients undergoing palate repair found palatine block demonstrated the greatest latency to first analgesia, but no difference in total opioid consumption for the former and bilateral infraorbital nerve blocks demonstrating the greatest latency to first analgesia and a mean decrease in morphine consumption for the latter.
Postoperative pain control in one RCT was best with rectal acetaminophen plus diclofenac vs. either drug alone or placebo.

Complications of nasoplasty at the time of cheiloplasty reported in a small case series of 86 patients were nasal tip infection (N = 4, often late occurring) and complications related to nostril conformers (N = 2).
Arm restraints do not appear beneficial post-operatively in terms of early complications and are not recommended by 2021 guidelines.
Guidelines recommend immediate breast or bottle feeding after cleft lip repair.
Feeding difficulties should be the main focus of care. Babies with CP have greater chance of growth failure than those with CL alone.

Breastfeeding may be difficult due to inability to properly position the areola. If breastfeeding is untenable, pumped breast milk offered through various cleft-specific commercial bottles should be encouraged. There are also various brands of nipples made specifically for babies with clefts.
In one small RCT of 57 infants, syringe feeding of breast milk was more effective than spoon feeding for weight gain at 10 and 14 weeks.

There is no statistically significant difference in weight gain between bottle types, although squeezable bottles were found easier to use than rigid bottles. There is also no statistically significance difference in weight gain between maxillary plate and no plate. There is some benefit to breastfeeding versus spoon feeding after palatal repair (about 0.5 kg greater weight at 6 weeks).
As noted above, immediate postoperative breastfeeding or bottle-feeding does not increase dehiscence following CL repair.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 19 studies concluded that speech and language therapy improved speech production to a clinically relevant degree for many individuals (95% CI 61- 87%) and that speech production was on a level with peers for some individuals after therapy (95% CI 10- 34%).

In an RCT with 14 children with speech difficulty from CP with or without CL, 10 hours of a linguistic-phonological approach was more effective than 10 hours of a traditional motor-phonetic approach with respect to correctly produced consonants and places although other scores were improved similarly in both groups.

In another small trial, high-intensity speech therapy (1 hour 5 times weekly for 2 weeks) was more effective than low-intensity speech therapy (1 hour weekly for 10 weeks) on speech understandability, acceptability, and total Velopharyngeal Insufficiency Effects on Life Outcomes scores.
Devices and masks

For children with unilateral CL/CP, use of nasoalveolar molding resulted in good to excellent frontal nasal form (RR 2.4, 95% CI 1.24-3.68) and vermillion border (RR 1.8, 95% CI 1.19-2.71) compared to nonuse of either molding or passive presurgical infant orthopedic appliances. However, there were no statistically significant differences in cephalometric measurements between these groups based on this meta-analysis of 12 studies.

Nasoalveolar molding with gingivoperiosteoplasty in a meta-analysis of 7 studies was successful in achieving continuity of alveolar bone structure in 71% (95% CI 54-85%) and potentially eliminated the need for future bone grafts.

A 12-year follow-up cohort study of children with bilateral CL-CP treated with presurgical nasoalveolar molding followed by primary lip/nasal reconstruction had uniformly good outcomes with nearly normal nasal morphology. In one RCT, there were similar nasal outcomes for two different nasoalveolar molding techniques.

In an RCT of 30 infants with bilateral CL/CP, both nasoalveolar molding and computer-aided design nasoalveolar molding decreased the intersegment cleft gap, but the later also caused more reduction in the total arch length by 1.99 mm.

Presurgical infant orthopedics (passive orthodontic plates or external traction devices to reduce the width of the bony cleft) has no apparent benefit including effect on growth or facial appearance. There are conflicting data on the effect of speech intelligibility after use of infant orthopedics.
Facemasks may be of some benefit on skeletal alignment in children with unilateral CL/CP based on a meta-analysis of 5 studies.

Horizontal taping (changed once daily) between the two labial segments at age 3 months, aiming to decrease the cleft gap before surgical lip repair, was useful for improving nose and lip aesthetics at 6 months of age as assessed by blinded reviewers in an RCT including 31 infants with nonsyndromic unilateral complete cleft lip and palate. There were no differences between the groups 2-weeks after surgery. Taping resulted in obvious irritation and inflammation in most infants around tape placement which sometimes developed into an open wound with bleeding.
For children with persistent articulation disorders, electropalatography has been recommended, but has not been studied in well designed clinical trials.

Botulinum toxin injections into the orbicularis oris muscle to reduce tension produced better appearing/narrower cleft lip repair scars on visual analogue scale, but no benefits with respect to scar pigmentation, vascularity, pliability, or height in one RCT. Similar results were found on VAS in a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs including 161 patients, however, there was no significant difference noted on the Vancouver Scar Scale.
Better scar appearance at 6 months was also demonstrated using botulinum toxin injections in an RCT of 22 (of 28) infants undergoing primary lip repair for unilateral CL.

The "team approach" to clefts appears optimal. A team consists of an operating surgeon, orthodontist, speech-language pathologist, otolaryngologist, audiologist, nutritionist, primary care physician, social worker, and, if a genetic syndrome is involved, a geneticist.
The ACPA has established standards for what constitutes the team and a directory is available.

In a systematic review, the incidence of fistula development following surgical repair was 8.6% (95% CI, 6.4%-11.1%). Fistulas were more common following combined cleft lip-cleft palate repair vs. cleft palate alone. There was no significant difference based on surgical repair technique, including a recent RCT comparing one-stage or two-stage palatoplasty in patients with complete unilateral CL/CP.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 464 children undergoing primary repair of the anterior palate using a single-layered, superiorly based, vomer mucoperiosteal flap found a lower fistula rate of 3% (95% CI: 1.0-9.0%) which did not differ by presence or absence of associated syndrome, single vs. multiple surgeons, or age at the time of cleft repair.
Midface hypoplasia is common after palatoplasty and has been hypothesized to be influenced by the timing of hard palate repair.
Scars resulting from cleft lip and/or palate (CL/P) repair surgeries can be improved with laser therapy.

Patients with CL/CP have an increased incidence of middle ear and other otorhinolaryngeal problems, necessitating referral to a craniofacial team including an ENT physician shortly after birth. In one case series of 319 patients, the incidence of OME accompanying cleft palate during palatoplasty was 72% in Asian patients.
In a systematic review of 9 studies, ventilation tube insertion vs. conservative treatment was beneficial for hearing recovery in children with CP and OME.

Children with CL/CP are at higher risk of dental caries and other oral disease due to factors including enamel hypoplasia, structural anomalies allowing trapped food particles, devices in the mouth that can become colonized with bacteria, and adverse effects of surgery on the blood supply to teeth or scaring in the oral vestibule impairing toothbrushing and flossing.

Children with CL and/or CP have an increased risk of maxillary deformities and dental occlusive disorders; patients with unilateral cleft have a greater chance of normal occlusion after correction. In 1 retrospective cohort study using completed surgery or arbitrarily set cephalometric criteria to identify need for surgery, 102 of 211 patients with complete unilateral CL and CP (48.3%) and 84 of 129 patients with complete bilateral CL and CP (65.1%) were deemed to benefit from orthognathic surgery (malposition of jaw). B In another RCT, maxillary distraction performed better than orthognathic surgery at 5 years.
There are conflicting data regarding the best surgical techniques and timing to minimize dental problems later in life.

Speech is affected in about 50% of children with CL and/or CP at age 5 years, and speech therapy is of benefit. Authors of a meta-analysis of 31 studies comparing 955 young children with non-syndromic CL/CP to 938 typically developing peers found significantly lower performance on measures of speech and language including less accurate articulation, more speech errors and poorer expressive and receptive language skills. These differences, however, appear to decrease with age.

Cross-sectional studies suggest that persons with nonsyndromal cleft lip and/or palates experience poorer cognitive functioning, most significantly in the language domain. Poorer cognitive ability was confirmed in a population-based study of children born with an oral cleft in England in which academic achievement at age 5 years was found to be significantly below national average. Differences were smallest for children who only had CL. Compared to a national rate of 9.7%, 13.2% of children with CL and 47.6% with bilateral CL/P had special educational needs.

Poorer academic performance was also shown in a meta-analysis of 16 studies. Children with non-syndromic orofacial clefts had a higher risk of academic underachievement than controls: OR 1.38 for CL (95% CI 1.20-1.57), OR 3.07 for CP (95% CI 2.65-3.56), and OR 3.96 for CL/CP (95% CI 3.31-4.72). In addition, reading problems have been documented compared to peers.
Children with CL/CP who are at an older age at palatoplasty and at first ventilation tube insertion, and who have more frequent insertion of ventilation tubes have poorer hearing outcomes.
Global health-related quality of life is slightly worse among individuals aged 8-19 years with cleft lip/palate compared to healthy controls.
Genetic karyotyping is probably not necessary for CL without associated anomalies.
Early surgical treatment appears best.

In a population study in Denmark, the recurrence risks for first-, second-, and third-degree relatives of a proband with CL and CP were 3.5% (95% CI, 3.1-4.0), 0.8% (0.6-1.0), and 0.6% (0.4-0.8), respectively.
